{"path":"effect_gouraud_shaded_cube_anthropic-claude-sonnet-5_01.html","edit_description":"
Create a complete, self-contained HTML file implementing a realtime Gouraud-shaded rotating cube using only Canvas 2D (no WebGL, no external libraries). Requirements:

1. Single HTML file with inline <style> and <script>, no external dependencies.
2. Canvas fills most of the viewport, dark background, centered.
3. Minimal 3D pipeline implemented manually:
   - Cube defined as 8 vertices in local space (side length ~1.5).
   - 6 faces, each defined as 4 vertex indices (quad), each face split into 2 triangles (so 12 triangles total), each triangle carries a face normal (computed from the untransformed face, one flat normal per face, used to compute per-vertex normals by averaging adjacent face normals per vertex for Gouraud interpolation across the face — implement smooth-ish per-vertex normals by summing the normals of faces sharing that vertex during setup).
   - Rotation matrices for X, Y, Z axes implemented as pure functions performing matrix multiplication on vertex vectors (rotation angles increase each frame using elapsed time, not fixed increments, so speed is independent of frame rate).
   - Perspective projection: after applying rotation and camera distance (translate cube away from camera along Z), project each vertex to 2D screen space using standard perspective divide (x' = x * f / z, y' = y * f / z) with a configurable field-of-view/focal length and the canvas center as origin offset.
   - Backface culling: after transforming to camera space, compute the transformed face normal (or use the cross product of two triangle edges in camera space) and cull triangles whose normal points away from the camera (dot product with view vector test), i.e. skip drawing triangles facing away.
4. Lighting:
   - A moving point light source: its position orbits around the cube over time (e.g. circular path with sin/cos of elapsed time, varying radius/height) so it visibly moves relative to the cube while the cube rotates.
   - Per-vertex Lambertian lighting: for each vertex of each triangle, compute the transformed vertex normal (rotated along with the cube, normalized), compute the light direction vector from the vertex to the moving light position (normalized), and set lighting intensity = max(0, dot(normal, lightDir)) plus a small ambient term (e.g. 0.15) so faces are never fully black, clamped to [0,1].
   - Each vertex has a base color (assign distinct hue per face for visual clarity, e.g. via HSL, or a single base color modulated per face) which is multiplied by the computed light intensity to get final per-vertex RGB color used for Gouraud interpolation.
5. Rasterization with Gouraud shading (manual, Canvas 2D pixel-level or scanline triangle fill — do NOT rely on canvas gradient/path fill tricks that fake it superficially; implement an actual scanline rasterizer):
   - For each visible (non-culled) triangle, sort its 3 projected 2D vertices by Y.
   - Use a standard scanline triangle-fill algorithm (edge-walking / barycentric interpolation) that, for each pixel row between the vertices, computes interpolated (r,g,b) color per pixel via linear interpolation along edges and across the scanline (true Gouraud shading, per-pixel color interpolation) and also interpolates depth (1/z or z) for a simple per-triangle depth check if useful, then writes pixels using either putImageData on an ImageData buffer (preferred, efficient) or many small fillRect/pixel draws.
   - Use an off-screen ImageData buffer for the frame, clear it each frame to background color, rasterize all visible triangles sorted back-to-front by average depth (painter's algorithm, since it's a single convex cube this is sufficient — no z-buffer required, but simple average-Z sort of triangles before drawing is required to get correct occlusion), then putImageData to canvas once per frame for performance.
   - Triangles must be filled with clipping to canvas bounds (clamp scanline x ranges and y ranges to canvas width/height to avoid out-of-bounds writes into the ImageData buffer).
6. Wireframe toggle: pressing 'W' or 'w' toggles a boolean; when true, additionally (or instead of filled shading) stroke each triangle/edge in a contrasting color (e.g. white or light gray semi-transparent lines) drawn via canvas stroke calls after the shaded raster (or instead of fill — toggling between solid Gouraud fill and wireframe-only outline mode is fine, pick whichever is cleaner, e.g. W toggles showing wireframe edges overlaid on top of the shaded faces, OR fully replaces fill with wireframe-only — implement as an overlay of white edges on top of the filled/shaded cube for best visual clarity).
7. Pause toggle: pressing 'P' or 'p' toggles a paused boolean; when paused, stop advancing rotation angle and light position time accumulation (freeze the animation) but keep rendering the last state; the requestAnimationFrame loop keeps running for FPS measurement but simulation time doesn't advance while paused.
8. FPS display: track frame timestamps (delta time between frames), compute a smoothed FPS (e.g. exponential moving average) and render it as text in the top-left corner of the canvas each frame (canvas fillText, e.g. white text with dark outline/shadow for readability), along with small on-screen instructions text (e.g. "W: wireframe  P: pause") also in a corner.
9. Use requestAnimationFrame for the render loop with proper delta-time based on performance.now().
10. Code must be vanilla JavaScript inside a <script> tag at the bottom of the body, well-commented explaining each pipeline stage (model->world rotation, camera/view transform, projection, backface culling, lighting, rasterization), clean readable formatting, no external libraries, no build step, works by opening directly in a browser.
11. Add a simple resize handler so canvas resizes with the window (recreate ImageData buffer on resize).
12. Give the page a title like "Gouraud Shaded Rotating Cube - Canvas 2D".

Produce the entire file content now.
"}
